\section[ābār]{\bn{আবার} (ābār) — \textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} the seed of \textquotedblleft{}see you again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C04-abar}



\begin{quote}
One small word turns a goodbye from \textquotedblleft{}farewell\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{till next time}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{আ}} (independent \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\bn{বা}} (\emph{bā}) + \textbf{\bn{র}} (\emph{r}) $\to$ \textbf{\bn{আবার}} (\emph{ābār}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{আবার}} (\emph{ābār}, \textquotedblleft{}again, once more\textquotedblright{}) is a native Indo-Aryan adverb with no tidy English cognate, but a familiar \emph{job}: it turns a parting into a promise. Chapter 1 gave you \textbf{\bn{আসি}} (\emph{āshi}, \textquotedblleft{}I'll come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}) as goodbye; add \emph{ābār} and you can say outright \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet \textbf{again}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}ābār\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} what it adds to a goodbye (\textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{āmi}, then read \textbf{\bn{কেমন}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ābār} mean, and what does it do to a farewell? (\textquotedblleft{}Again\textquotedblright{}; it makes the parting a promise of return.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dækhā hôbe]{\bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে} (dækhā hôbe) — \textquotedblleft{}(we) will meet\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C04-dekha-hobe}



\begin{quote}
A future-tense phrase — the other half of \textquotedblleft{}see you again,\textquotedblright{} built in a way English never would.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{দেখা}} (\emph{dækhā}, \textquotedblleft{}seeing\textquotedblright{}) = \textbf{\bn{দে}} (\emph{dæ}) + \textbf{\bn{খা}} (\emph{khā}). \textbf{\bn{হবে}} (\emph{hôbe}, \textquotedblleft{}will be/happen\textquotedblright{}) = \textbf{\bn{হ}} (\emph{hô}) + \textbf{\bn{বে}} (\emph{be}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}a{]} seeing will happen}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dækhā} (the noun \textquotedblleft{}seeing,\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{\bn{দেখা}} \emph{dækhā} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{hôbe} (\textquotedblleft{}will be/happen,\textquotedblright{} the future of \textbf{\bn{হওয়া}} \emph{hôwā}, \textquotedblleft{}to be, to become\textquotedblright{}). Bengali says \textquotedblleft{}a meeting will occur\textquotedblright{} rather than \textquotedblleft{}we will meet\textquotedblright{} — an impersonal, gentle way to promise reunion. The verb \emph{hôwā} (\textquotedblleft{}to be/become\textquotedblright{}) is the same one behind \emph{āchhā}'s cousin, and its root \textbf{\bn{ভূ} / \bn{হ}} ties (distantly) to English \textbf{be}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the impersonal future}]
Many Bengali \textquotedblleft{}we'll…\textquotedblright{} expressions use this \textbf{noun + hôbe} (\textquotedblleft{}…will happen\textquotedblright{}) shape: \emph{dækhā hôbe} (\textquotedblleft{}{[}a{]} seeing will happen\textquotedblright{}), \emph{kôthā hôbe} (\textquotedblleft{}{[}a{]} talk will happen\textquotedblright{}). No \textquotedblleft{}we,\textquotedblright{} no active verb — the event itself is the subject.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}dækhā hôbe\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} its literal meaning (\textquotedblleft{}{[}a{]} seeing will happen\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{Say it:} the verb \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} inside it (\emph{dækhā})
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bhālo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{dækhā hôbe} literally say, and what is odd (to English ears) about it? (\textquotedblleft{}A seeing will happen\textquotedblright{}; it is impersonal — the \emph{event} is the subject, not \textquotedblleft{}we.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ābār dækhā hôbe]{\bn{আবার} \bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে} (ābār dækhā hôbe) — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C04-abar-dekha-hobe}



\begin{quote}
The warm, everyday goodbye — the fuller cousin of Chapter 1's \emph{āshi}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{আবার} \bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} = \textbf{\bn{আবার}} (\emph{ābār}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} (\emph{dækhā hôbe}, \textquotedblleft{}{[}a{]} seeing will happen\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we'll meet again}\textquotedblright{} (literally \textquotedblleft{}again a seeing will happen\textquotedblright{}). Chapter 1 gave you the tender \textbf{\bn{আসি}} (\emph{āshi}, \textquotedblleft{}I'll come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}), the \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} goodbye; \emph{ābār dækhā hôbe} is its warm, explicit form. It is the sibling of the whole subcontinent's parting habit (Hindi \emph{phir milenge}, Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}): never a blunt \textquotedblleft{}goodbye,\textquotedblright{} always a return promised.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the warm goodbye — \emph{ābār dækhā hôbe}
  \item the two pieces (\emph{ābār} + \emph{dækhā hôbe})
  \item the Chapter-1 goodbye it deepens (\emph{āshi})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ābār dækhā hôbe} literally say, and how does it relate to \emph{āshi}? (\textquotedblleft{}Again a seeing will happen\textquotedblright{}; it is the fuller, explicit form of Ch.1's \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} goodbye.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāl dækhā hôbe]{\bn{কাল} \bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে} (kāl dækhā hôbe) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C04-kal-dekha-hobe}



\begin{quote}
A goodbye for tomorrow — built on a word that means both \textbf{tomorrow} and \textbf{yesterday}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{কা}} (\emph{kā}) + \textbf{\bn{ল}} (\emph{l}) $\to$ \textbf{\bn{কাল}} (\emph{kāl}). Two simple letters, one tricky word.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{কাল}} (\emph{kāl}) means \textbf{both \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{}} — the day on either side of today — from Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{কাল}} (\emph{kāla}, \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}). (It is the very same \emph{kāla} behind Hindi's \emph{kal} and Punjabi's \emph{akāl} \textquotedblleft{}timeless.\textquotedblright{}) Bengali trusts the verb's tense to tell which: \emph{kāl dækhā hôbe} (future $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow}\textquotedblright{}), \emph{kāl dækhā hôyechhilo} (past $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yesterday}\textquotedblright{}). So \textbf{\bn{কাল} \bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} = \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow, a seeing will happen\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kāl dækhā hôbe\textquotedblright{}
  \item the puzzle — \emph{kāl} means both \textbf{tomorrow} and \textbf{yesterday}
  \item the root and its cousins (\emph{kāla} \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}; Hindi \emph{kal}, Punjabi \emph{akāl})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two opposite days does \emph{kāl} mean, and what tells them apart? (Both tomorrow and yesterday; the verb's tense.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 7 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:BN-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three ways to part — none of them a blunt \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the tender Chapter-1 goodbye — \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{})
  \item the fuller \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ābār dækhā hôbe}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kāl dækhā hôbe}
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\begin{cousinweb}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}{[}a{]} seeing will happen\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ābār}, \emph{dækhā hôbe})
  \item the word that means BOTH tomorrow and yesterday (\emph{kāl})
  \item what's odd about \emph{dækhā hôbe} (impersonal — the event is the subject)
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dækhā hôbe} — \textquotedblleft{}{[}a{]} seeing will happen\textquotedblright{}; the impersonal future
  \item \emph{kāl} $\leftarrow$ \emph{kāla} \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} (Hindi \emph{kal}, Punjabi \emph{akāl})
  \item \emph{āshi} (Ch.1) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll come {[}again{]},\textquotedblright{} the Bengali promise-of-return goodbye
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You're leaving a friend and expect to see them next week. Which goodbye fits, and how does Bengali phrase \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Ābār dækhā hôbe}; impersonally — \textquotedblleft{}a seeing will happen.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(practice)]{Four exchanges, and two ways to leave}

\label{lesson:BN-R08-second-pass-four-exchanges}



\begin{quote}
Four chapters, four exchanges, each practised once in the chapter that taught it. From memory: the first thing you say on meeting someone, and the last thing you say on leaving.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the two goodbyes differ by one word}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{আবার} \bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} & we'll meet again \\
\textbf{\bn{কাল} \bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} & see you tomorrow \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} — \textquotedblleft{}a meeting will happen\textquotedblright{} — does the work in both. What changes is the one word in front: \emph{again}, or \emph{tomorrow}. Neither goodbye says \emph{goodbye}; both name the next meeting, and the front word is how far off it is.

\textbf{\bn{কাল}} is the one to keep an eye on. It is the same word for \emph{yesterday} and \emph{tomorrow}, and only the verb around it tells you which way time is running.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the greeting exchange, both voices
  \item ask how someone is, and answer
  \item give your name, and ask for theirs
  \item leave someone you will see tomorrow, then someone you may not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do both goodbyes share? (\textbf{\bn{দেখা} \bn{হবে}} — a meeting will happen.) What changes between them? (\textbf{The word in front} — again, or tomorrow.) What is odd about \textbf{\bn{কাল}}? (\textbf{It is also \emph{yesterday}}.) And what tells you which one is meant? (\textbf{The verb around it.})
\end{tcolorbox}
